unit.title: Prepare dishes using basic methods of cookery

summary: This unit teaches you the basic methods of cookery and how to choose the right one for each food: moist heat (boiling, simmering, poaching, steaming, stewing, braising, pressure cooking), dry heat (roasting, baking, grilling) and fat-based methods (sautéing, shallow and deep frying, stir-frying). You learn how heat cooks food, how to control it safely, how to tell when food is done, and how to cook Jamaican dishes by each method.

blocks.p: Every dish you will ever cook is made with one or more of a small number of methods. If you understand the methods, you can cook a dish you have never seen before: you know what the heat does to the food, how long it takes, what can go wrong and how to know when it is ready. This unit is for HOSPITALITY VILLA/PROPERTIES SERVICES LEVEL 2 trainees.

Cooking is also the most dangerous part of kitchen work, because it uses fire, hot oil, steam and sharp tools, and because under-cooked food can make guests ill. So this unit keeps **safety, temperature and timing** in front of you as you learn each method.

blocks.note: How you are assessed: theory papers (multiple-choice questions, short answers and essays) and group practical tasks in the Centre's kitchen: one cooking Jamaican food by moist heat (brown stew chicken, steamed callaloo, boiled food) and one by dry heat and frying (jerk chicken, fried fish, festival, sautéed vegetables). The assessor watches your food safety, heat control, safety and plating, as well as the food.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.h: Hygiene and food safety while you cook

ul: Wash your hands before work, after raw meat, bins and the toilet, and between tasks. Wear a clean apron and hair cover; cover cuts with a coloured waterproof plaster and a glove.
Keep raw and cooked food apart: separate colour-coded boards and knives, and wash hands after raw meat.
Bacteria grow fastest in the **danger zone**, about **5 °C to 63 °C**. Cook through quickly, hold hot food at 63 °C or above, and chill cooked food fast.

Cook chicken, minced meat and reheated food to a **core temperature of about 74 °C**, measured in the thickest part with a clean probe thermometer. Follow the Centre's food safety plan if it gives a different figure.
Taste with a clean spoon, and use a fresh spoon each time.
Every food handler in Jamaica needs a Food Handler's Permit from the local health department.

blocks.h: Dangers in the kitchen and how you prevent them

head: Danger
Prevent it by
rows: Burns and scalds from pans, ovens, oil, steam and boiling liquids
Dry oven cloths (wet cloth carries heat)
Pan handles turned inwards
Lift lids away from your face
Never carry a full pot of hot liquid through a busy kitchen; shout 'hot' and ask for help
Cuts from knives and equipment
The right knife, kept sharp
A steady board; curled fingers
Carry knives point down; never catch a falling knife
Wash knives one at a time
Slips and falls
Wipe spills at once; wet-floor sign
Non-slip, closed shoes
No cables or boxes in walkways
Fire
Never leave hot oil alone
Keep cloths and paper away from flames
Know where the fire blanket, extinguisher and gas shut-off are
Gas leaks
If you smell gas: switch off, open windows, leave and report; no switches, no flames
Electric shock
Dry hands; keep cables away from water; report cracked plugs
Strains
Bend your knees to lift; ask for help with heavy pots

flow: Turn off the heat, if you can do so safely
Smother the flames: slide a lid, a baking tray or a fire blanket over the pan
Leave it covered; do not lift the cover or move the pan
Raise the alarm and use the right extinguisher only if you are trained and the fire spreads
Let the oil cool for a long time before moving it
Report the fire and what caused it

blocks.note: **Never throw water on an oil or fat fire.** Water sinks below the oil, turns to steam in an instant and throws burning oil all over the kitchen. Never carry a burning pan.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.note: Many Jamaican kitchens use LPG gas. Learn where the cylinder valve is, check that hoses are not cracked, and never store a spare cylinder indoors near heat. In Jamaica's hot weather, check that the kitchen has good air flow, because heat and fumes build up quickly.
blocks.label: Jamaica

sections.title: How food cooks and how to choose a method

head: Way heat travels
What happens
Kitchen example
rows: Conduction
Heat passes from a hot surface or liquid into the food that touches it.
A steak on a hot pan; heat moving from the outside of a roast to the centre.
Convection
Hot air or liquid moves round the food.
Water circulating in a boiling pot; a fan oven.
Radiation
Heat travels in rays from a hot source, without touching.
A grill or salamander browning food; charcoal.

ul: **Proteins** (meat, fish, eggs) set (coagulate) and turn firm. Overcooking makes them dry and tough.
**Tough meat** has connective tissue (collagen). Long, slow, moist cooking turns it into soft jelly, so the meat becomes tender. That is why oxtail, goat and tough cuts are stewed.
**Starches** in rice, flour and root vegetables take in water and swell and soften (gelatinise).
**Vegetables** soften as their cell walls break down. Green vegetables lose their bright colour if overcooked; water-soluble vitamins escape into the cooking water.

**Browning** happens when the surface of food reaches about 150 °C or more in dry heat or fat. It makes new flavours and colours. Moist heat cannot go above 100 °C (at sea level), so boiled food does not brown.
Cooking kills most harmful bacteria, if the centre of the food gets hot enough.

head: Group
Cooks the food in
Methods
Typical result
rows: Moist heat
Water, stock, milk or steam (up to about 100 °C)
Boiling, simmering, poaching, steaming, stewing, braising, blanching, pressure cooking
Soft, tender, juicy; no browning
Dry heat
Hot air or radiated heat, with little or no liquid
Roasting, baking, grilling, barbecuing
Browned, crisp outside, tender inside
Fat-based
Hot fat or oil
Sautéing, stir-frying, shallow frying, deep frying
Browned, crisp outside, often quick

blocks.p: Ask three questions: **What is the food?** (a tough cut or a tender one, a delicate fish or a root vegetable), **what result do I want?** (soft, crisp, juicy, browned) and **how much time do I have?**

head: Food
Good methods
Why
rows: Tough cuts: oxtail, goat, cow foot, stewing beef
Stewing, braising, pressure cooking
Long, slow, moist heat softens the connective tissue.
Tender cuts: chicken pieces, pork chops, steaks
Roasting, grilling, frying, sautéing
They stay tender with a shorter cooking time.
Delicate fish
Steaming, poaching, shallow frying, light grilling
Gentle heat stops it falling apart.
Green leaves: callaloo, pak choi
Steaming, sweating, quick sauté
Short cooking keeps the colour and vitamins.
Root vegetables and green bananas
Boiling, steaming, roasting, frying
They need to cook until the starch is soft.
Eggs
Boiling, poaching, frying, baking
Different results from the same food.
Dough: bread, buns, cakes
Baking; festival and dumplings: frying or boiling
Heat sets the dough.

ul: A **heavy-based pot**, such as a Dutch pot, spreads heat evenly and holds it. It is best for stews and rice and peas, which can burn on a thin base.
A **thin saucepan** heats quickly; it is good for boiling and simmering, but food scorches easily.
A **steamer** or a pot with a basket holds food above the water.
A **frying pan** or **wok** for sautéing and stir-frying; a **deep pot or fryer** for deep frying.
A **roasting tray** with a rack lifts meat out of its own fat.
Choose a size that is not much bigger than the food. Too large a pot spreads the food thin and it scorches; too small a pot overcrowds it.

head: Method
How it is done
Temperature
Good for
Take care
rows: Boiling
Food cooked in plenty of water at a full boil: big, rolling bubbles.
About 100 °C at sea level (a little lower in the hills)
Green bananas, yam, eggs, pasta, rice (some methods)
Do not overcook. Boiling hard breaks delicate food up and loses vitamins. Hot water scalds.
Simmering
Liquid just below boiling: small bubbles break the surface now and then.
About 85 to 95 °C
Soups, stews, stocks, rice and peas, dumplings
Keep the heat low and steady. A hard boil makes meat tough and sauces split.
Poaching
Food covered in liquid that barely moves, with no bubbles.
About 70 to 85 °C
Eggs, fish fillets, fruit
Handle gently; keep the heat low.
Steaming
Food above boiling water in a basket or steamer with a lid; the food does not touch the water.
About 100 °C
Callaloo, fish, carrots, pumpkin
Keep the water level up, not touching the food. Lift lids away from your face.
Stewing
Small pieces of food covered in liquid, cooked slowly in a covered pot.
Gentle simmer
Brown stew chicken, curry goat, oxtail, stewed peas
Brown first for flavour; keep covered; stir to stop sticking.
Braising
A large piece of food cooked slowly in a covered pot with liquid coming only part-way up.
Gentle simmer (stove or oven)
Whole cuts of beef, large pieces of meat
Turn the meat part-way; keep covered.
Blanching
Food boiled briefly, then cooled at once in cold water.
Boiling, then cold
Loosening skins (tomatoes), setting the colour of green vegetables, preparing food to freeze
Do not leave it in the water too long.
Pressure cooking
Food cooked in a sealed pot where steam pressure raises the temperature above 100 °C, so it cooks much faster.
Often about 115 to 120 °C
Dried peas and beans, tough meats such as oxtail and cow foot
See below.

blocks.p: **Boiling** has big, rolling bubbles and moves food about. **Simmering** has a few small bubbles and is gentler, so meat stays tender and sauces stay smooth. Most recipes that say 'bring to the boil, then simmer' mean you should lower the heat as soon as the liquid boils. Salt is added to the water for vegetables and for boiled root crops; follow the recipe for when to salt beans.

blocks.h: Steaming: why it is a healthy method

ul: The food does not sit in water, so fewer vitamins and minerals are lost.
No fat is added.
Colour, shape and flavour are kept, as long as the food is not overcooked.
To steam: bring a little water to the boil, check it does not touch the food, add the food in a single layer, cover and cook until just tender.

blocks.p: Stewing covers the food with liquid; braising, partly. Both use low heat for a long time. For brown stew chicken, season well, marinate, brown the pieces in hot oil (so they gain colour and flavour), add onion, pepper, tomato and a little liquid, cover and simmer gently until tender, stirring now and then. Do not overcrowd the pot when browning, or the meat will steam in its own juices and turn grey.

ul: Check that the vent, the valve and the rubber ring (gasket) are clean and undamaged.
Add the liquid the maker says. Do not fill above about two-thirds of the pot, and only half for foods that foam or swell, such as beans and rice.
Lock the lid; heat until the pressure builds, then lower the heat to hold the pressure and start the timer.
At the end, let the pressure drop fully by itself, or use the maker's release method. **Do not force the lid**. If it will not turn, there is still pressure inside.
Open the lid away from your face, as steam can scald.
Wash the lid and valve after use and store with the lid upside down.

head: Term
What it is
How to do it
rows: Stock
A flavoured liquid made by simmering bones or vegetables, used as a base for soups, stews and sauces.
Cover bones and vegetables with cold water, bring slowly to a simmer (never a hard boil), skim off scum, simmer: chicken 1 to 2 hours, beef 3 to 4 hours, then strain and cool quickly.
Mirepoix
A mix of chopped onion, carrot and celery used to flavour stocks and stews (roughly 2 parts onion to 1 each of carrot and celery).
Cut the pieces to a similar size so they cook together.
Jamaican seasoning base
Escallion, thyme, pimento, garlic, onion and sweet pepper, with scotch bonnet for heat.
Used for most stews, soups, rice and peas and jerk.
Sweating
Cooking vegetables gently in a little fat with a lid on, until soft and glossy but not brown.
Use low heat; stir now and then. Onions turn translucent.
Roux
Flour cooked with an equal amount of fat; used to thicken sauces.
Cook out the raw flour taste; add warm liquid slowly, stirring to avoid lumps; simmer for about 10 minutes.

blocks.note: Never put a very hot, large pot of stock into the fridge. Cool it fast: divide it into shallow trays, or stand the pot in a sink of iced water and stir, then chill.
blocks.label: Safety

head: Method
How it is done
Good for
Take care
rows: Roasting
Food cooked in the dry heat of an oven, usually with fat and often basted.
Whole chicken, joints of meat, vegetables
Preheat the oven. Do not open the door often. Check the core temperature.
Baking
Cooking in the dry heat of an oven; mostly used for bread, cakes, pastry and puddings.
Bread, buns, cakes, pastry, baked fish
Right temperature and shelf; do not open the door early on cakes.
Grilling
Cooking quickly with strong radiant heat from above or below.
Chops, fish, sausages, toast, browning the top of a dish
Watch closely; it burns fast. Turn the food. Keep fat from dripping and flaring.
Barbecuing and jerk
Cooking over charcoal or wood, often seasoned or marinated, slowly.
Jerk chicken and pork, fish, sausages
Control the heat; do not leave unattended; handle charcoal safely.

flow: Preheat the oven (often about 180 to 200 °C; follow the recipe)
Prepare the chicken on the raw-meat board; remove giblets; wash hands
Season well, inside and out, and rub with a little oil
Place on a rack or on sliced onions in a roasting tray, so heat reaches all round
Roast, basting now and then with the hot fat and juices
Check the core temperature in the thickest part of the thigh with a probe thermometer: about 74 °C
Rest for 10 to 15 minutes, loosely covered, then carve

ul: **Basting** means spooning the hot fat or juices over the food to keep it moist and help it brown.
**Resting** lets the juices settle back into the meat, so they do not pour out when you carve, and the meat stays moist and easier to carve.
Use the juices in the tray for a gravy: pour off the extra fat, stir in a little roux or a cornflour mix, add stock, simmer and season.
Many kitchens preheat the oven for 15 to 20 minutes. Check that the oven temperature is right with an oven thermometer, because ovens differ.

blocks.p: Both use an oven, and the difference is mostly in what is cooked and the language. **Roasting** is for meat, poultry and vegetables, usually with fat. **Baking** is mostly for bread, cakes, pastry and other food made from dough or batter. In some recipes the words are used for the same thing, such as baked fish or roast potatoes.

**Jerk** is a Jamaican way of seasoning meat with a spicy paste or marinade of scotch bonnet pepper, pimento (allspice), escallion, thyme, garlic and other spices, and then cooking it slowly, traditionally over pimento wood and charcoal. At the Centre, jerk chicken may be roasted in the oven or grilled on a safe outdoor grill. The chicken must be cooked right through to about 74 °C, because the spicy outside can look cooked while the inside is not.

blocks.note: Wear gloves when you handle scotch bonnet pepper, and do not touch your eyes, nose or mouth. Wash your hands, board and knife afterwards.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.note: A salamander is a professional overhead grill used to brown or finish food from above. Dishes put under it must not be left, and the plate and the rim will be very hot.
blocks.label: Tip

ul: Use dry, thick oven cloths and open the door slowly, standing to the side, because hot air and steam rush out.
Pull the shelf out a little before lifting a tray. Never reach in deep.
Put hot trays on a heat-proof stand, not directly on the bench.

head: Method
How it is done
Good for
rows: Sautéing
Cooking small or thin pieces of food quickly in a little hot fat in a shallow pan, tossing or turning them.
Sliced vegetables, thin cuts of meat or fish, onions
Stir-frying
Cooking small pieces very quickly in a very hot wok or pan, stirring all the time.
Vegetables, strips of meat, noodles
Shallow frying
Cooking in a layer of fat about half-way up the food, turning once.
Fish, fritters, dumplings, plantain, eggs
Deep frying
Cooking food fully covered in hot oil.
Festival, fish, chips, fritters, bammy

ul: The oil must be **hot enough** before the food goes in. The outside seals quickly, which makes it crisp and stops the food soaking up too much oil. For deep frying most foods, the oil is commonly about **170 to 190 °C**. Follow the recipe and the fryer maker's guide.
Do not overload the pan or basket. Too much cold food drops the oil temperature, so the food cooks slowly and absorbs oil and comes out pale and greasy. Fry in batches and let the oil heat up again.

**Dry the food** with kitchen paper first. Wet food makes oil spit and splash. A coating of flour, batter, or flour, egg and breadcrumbs (called **pané**) protects delicate food, such as fish, and makes a crisp outside.
Drain fried food on kitchen paper or a rack, and salt it while it is hot.
Do not let oil smoke: smoking oil is too hot, is breaking down and can catch fire.

flow: Check the fryer or pot is clean and dry
Fill with fresh or well-filtered oil to the fill line; in a pot, no more than about half full
Heat to the temperature in the recipe, using the thermostat or a thermometer
Dry the food; coat if the recipe says
Lower the food in gently, **away from you**, a few pieces at a time
Cook until golden and cooked through; lift out and drain
Wait for the oil to come back to temperature before the next batch
Switch off, let the oil cool fully, then strain and cover, or dispose of it

ul: Filter the oil after use through a fine strainer or filter paper to remove crumbs, which burn and spoil it.
Change the oil when it is **dark, foams, smells bad or smokes** at a lower temperature than it used to. Old oil gives food a bad taste and can be a fire risk.
Do not mix old and new oil, and do not use the same oil for fish and then for sweet items; flavours transfer.
Never pour used oil down the sink: let it cool, store it in a labelled, lidded container and have it collected as the Centre arranges.

blocks.note: Never leave hot oil alone, not even for a minute. Never fill a pot more than half full. Never move a pot of hot oil. Never let water near hot oil, and keep a lid or fire blanket close by.
blocks.label: Safety

ul: Heat the pan first, then add a little oil, then the food.
Cut the food to a similar size so it cooks evenly.
Do not crowd the pan: cook in batches or the food will stew in its own juices.
Add the food that takes longest first (carrot before sweet pepper).
Toss or stir often so the food does not burn.

blocks.p: Jamaican cooking uses all the basic methods. The table shows which method a dish uses, and the main points to remember.

head: Dish
Method
Key points
rows: Brown stew chicken
Stewing (after browning)
Season and marinate; brown in batches; simmer covered for 30 to 40 minutes; chicken reaches about 74 °C; gravy thickens.
Oxtail with butter beans
Stewing, or pressure cooking
Tough cut: long, slow, moist cooking; the beans go in late so they stay whole.
Curry goat
Stewing
Season with curry powder and thyme, brown, then simmer slowly until tender; a tough cut takes 1 to 2 hours or more.
Rice and peas
Simmering and steaming in a covered pot
Boil kidney beans hard for at least 10 minutes, then simmer until soft; cook the rice in the bean liquid with coconut milk; keep the lid on and rest.
Boiled green bananas, yam and dumplings (spinners)
Boiling
Salted water; test with a knife; do not overcook. Spinners are small, finger-shaped dumplings.
Steamed callaloo
Steaming or sweating
Short cooking until just tender; keeps colour and goodness.
Steamed fish with okra
Steaming
Season; layer with okra, onion, carrot, thyme, escallion and pimento; steam until the flesh is opaque and flakes.
Ackee and saltfish
Boiling (saltfish, ackee), then sautéing
Make the ackee safe first; boil saltfish to remove salt; fold in the ackee gently at the end.
Escoveitch fish
Frying, then pickling
Dry, season, flour and fry the fish until crisp; pour over a hot dressing of vinegar, onion, carrot, sweet pepper and scotch bonnet, with a few pimento berries.
Run down
Simmering
Fish or mackerel simmered in coconut milk with onion, tomato, thyme and pepper until the milk reduces to a thick, oily sauce.
Jerk chicken
Roasting, grilling or barbecuing
Marinate well; cook slowly; check 74 °C in the thickest part.
Festival
Deep frying
Stiff dough shaped like fingers; fry until golden; drain.
Bammy
Frying or steaming
Made from grated cassava that is squeezed to remove the liquid; flat rounds fried or steamed.
Pumpkin soup
Simmering, then blending
Simmer pumpkin with seasoning until soft; blend in small amounts with the lid on; reheat until piping hot.

blocks.note: Cassava (the root used for bammy) contains a natural poison in its raw form, especially bitter types. It is made safe by grating, squeezing out the juice and cooking. Do not eat raw cassava, and use cassava that has been properly processed.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.note: Coconut milk splits or curdles if it is boiled hard for a long time. Simmer it gently and stir now and then, especially when cooking run down.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: Only ripe ackee from pods that have **opened naturally on the tree** is safe. Unripe or forced-open ackee contains a poison called hypoglycin. Remove the black seeds and the pink-red membrane from each piece, wash it, and boil it gently, then throw the water away. Canned ackee from an approved source is ready to heat.

sections.title: Checking, seasoning, serving and cleaning down

blocks.h: How to tell when food is cooked

head: Food
It is ready when
rows: Chicken, minced meat, sausage, reheated food
The core temperature is about 74 °C in the thickest part, and the juices run clear.
Beef or goat stew
A fork goes in easily and the meat nearly falls apart.
Fish
The flesh is opaque (not see-through), firm and flakes easily when pressed. Fish needs less time than meat.
Boiled vegetables and root vegetables
A knife goes in easily. Green vegetables are still bright and keep their shape.
Rice
The liquid is absorbed and the grains are tender and separate.
Pasta
Just firm to the bite: **al dente**.
Eggs
As the recipe says: set whites for boiled or poached eggs, with the yolk to the guest's wishes.
Deep-fried food
Golden brown, crisp outside and cooked in the middle (cut one open to check).
Cakes and bread
Risen, golden, and springy to the touch; a clean skewer comes out dry.

ul: Season in stages and taste each time with a clean spoon; you can add salt but you cannot take it out.
Taste for salt, heat, sweetness and sourness, and for the balance between them.
Add salt later in dishes that are reduced, as the flavour gets stronger.
Fresh herbs go in at the end for flavour; dried herbs earlier.
Hot food is held at 63 °C or above, covered, and served as soon as possible.
Plates for hot food are clean and warm, never cold and never too hot to hold. Wipe the rim of the plate.
Balance colour: green callaloo, orange carrot, golden festival. Add a garnish that is edible and suits the dish.
Give each guest the right portion, using the same ladle, scoop or weight each time.

blocks.p: Cool leftovers quickly in shallow trays, cover, label with the name, date and time, and chill. Rice needs particular care, because a bacterium in rice can make a poison that reheating does not destroy. Reheat once, to about 74 °C, until piping hot.

flow: Switch off the gas or electric; let hot things cool
Scrape and wash pots, pans and tools in hot soapy water; rinse
Sanitise food-contact surfaces and leave them to air-dry
Clean the stove top, wipe the oven and the work surfaces
Let oil cool; strain and cover it
Sweep and mop with a wet-floor sign
Put food away, labelled; report faults

blocks.note: Never mix bleach with other cleaners, because the mix can give off a poisonous gas. Read the label and follow the maker's instructions and the Centre's rules.
blocks.label: Safety

ul: I can name the danger zone and the safe temperatures for cooking, holding and storing food.
I can prevent burns, cuts, slips and fires, and I know what to do if oil catches fire.
I can explain how conduction, convection and radiation cook food.
I can name the three groups of methods and give two methods and a dish for each.
I can choose a method and a pot to suit the food, and explain why tough cuts are stewed.
I can explain the difference between boiling, simmering and poaching.
I can steam food and say why steaming is a healthy method.
I can explain stewing and braising, and brown stew chicken step by step.
I can use a pressure cooker safely.
I can describe stock, mirepoix, sweating and roux.
I can roast a chicken, and explain basting and resting.
I can explain the difference between roasting and baking, and between grilling and jerk.
I can control oil temperature, avoid overloading, and fry safely.
I can say when frying oil must be changed.
I can make the ackee safe, and cook ackee and saltfish.
I can cook rice and peas, boiled food, callaloo, escoveitch fish and run down.
I can tell when food is cooked, season and taste with a clean spoon, and plate it.
I can cool leftovers, clean down and report faults.

blocks.note: In essay answers, give the reason for each step: 'I pat the fish dry before frying, so that the oil does not spit and burn me.'
blocks.label: Tip

terms: Having everything prepared and in its place before you cook.
The temperature range of about 5 °C to 63 °C where bacteria grow fastest.
The temperature in the thickest part of the food.
Heat passing from a hot surface or liquid into food that touches it.
Heat carried by moving hot air or liquid.
Heat travelling in rays from a hot source.
Cooking in water, stock or steam.
Cooking in hot air or radiated heat, with little liquid.
Cooking in liquid at a full boil, with big bubbles (about 100 °C at sea level).
Cooking in liquid just below boiling, with small bubbles.
Cooking gently in liquid that is not bubbling.
Cooking in the steam above boiling water.
Slow cooking of small pieces covered in liquid.
Slow cooking of a large piece with liquid part-way up.
Boiling briefly, then cooling at once in cold water.
A sealed pot where steam pressure cooks food faster at a higher temperature.
A flavoured liquid made by simmering bones or vegetables.
Chopped onion, carrot and celery used to flavour stocks and stews.
Cooking vegetables gently in a little fat, with a lid, until soft but not brown.
Flour cooked with fat, used to thicken a sauce.
Cooking in the dry heat of an oven, usually with fat.
Cooking in the dry heat of an oven; mostly bread, cakes and pastry.
Spooning hot fat or juices over food as it cooks.
Cooking quickly with strong radiant heat from above or below.
A professional overhead grill used to brown food from above.
A Jamaican spicy seasoning, and the slow cooking of meat seasoned with it.
Cooking quickly in a little hot fat, tossing or turning the food.
Cooking small pieces very quickly in a hot wok, stirring constantly.
Cooking food fully covered in hot oil.
A coating of flour, beaten egg and breadcrumbs.
Cooked but still firm to the bite.

c1.title: Oxtail in the pressure cooker in Montego Bay
c1.text: Trainee Davene is cooking oxtail with butter beans for the staff lunch at a hotel in Montego Bay. She browns the seasoned oxtail, then puts it in the pressure cooker with water filled right to the top rim and locks the lid. After 45 minutes she switches off the heat. The lunch is late, and she tries to turn the lid at once, but it will not move.

c2.title: Frying snapper in Negril
c2.text: At a villa in Negril, Chef Winston deep-fries snapper for escoveitch. He tips twelve fillets straight from the marinade into a pot of oil at 180 °C. The oil spits, the temperature drops and the fish comes out pale and greasy. The oil is dark and foams a little, and the pot is about three-quarters full. He then pours a hot mixture of vinegar, onion, carrot, sweet pepper and scotch bonnet over the fish.

c3.title: Roast chicken for a function in Kingston
c3.text: Chef Marva roasts 12 chicken leg quarters in a hotel kitchen in Kingston for a function that starts in 10 minutes. The skin is golden, but the probe reads 68 °C in the thickest part of the largest piece. She has packed the pieces tightly in one deep tray, so they overlap.

c4.title: Callaloo and run down in Port Antonio
c4.text: At a guest house in Port Antonio, trainee Neville boils callaloo in a big pot of salted water for 25 minutes. It comes out grey, watery and tasteless. The chef tells him to steam it. Later he cooks run down: he turns the heat high so the coconut milk boils hard, and it begins to split.

c5.title: Curry goat in St Elizabeth
c5.text: Trainee Janelle simmers curry goat for 40 minutes at a hotel in St Elizabeth. The meat is still tough and the sauce is thin. She wants to turn up the heat and boil hard to finish quickly. The goat was cut into small pieces and browned before the liquid went in.

c6.title: A flare-up in an Ocho Rios kitchen
c6.text: In a hotel kitchen in Ocho Rios, a pan of oil on a gas ring catches fire. Trainee Keisha grabs a jug of water. A cook beside her shouts for her to stop. A fire blanket hangs on the wall by the door.

questions.q: Why is oxtail cooked by stewing or in a pressure cooker?
o: Dry heat makes the bone give off more flavour
A quick, hot cook seals the juices inside the meat
The fat in the bone melts only above 200 °C
Long, moist heat softens its tough tissue
questions.why: Oxtail is a tough cut with a lot of connective tissue (collagen). Long, slow, moist cooking, or the higher heat of a pressure cooker, turns it into soft jelly and makes the meat tender.

questions.q: What is wrong with filling the pressure cooker to the rim?
o: The oxtail will need much longer, as there is more water to heat
Foam can block the vent, so fill no more than two-thirds
The lid will not seal, so the steam escapes from its sides
The butter beans will stay hard, because the water is too deep
questions.why: A cooker needs space above the food for steam. Over-filling lets foam or liquid block the vent and valve, which is dangerous. Foods that foam or swell, such as beans, need even more room.

questions.q: The lid will not turn after the heat is switched off. What does this tell Davene?
o: The lid is stuck and needs extra force to free it
The meat is cooked and has stuck to the lid
There is still pressure inside, so she must wait
The cooker is faulty and must be thrown away
questions.why: A lid that will not turn means pressure is still in the pot. Forcing it can release scalding steam and food. Wait until the pressure has dropped fully, or use the maker's release method, and open the lid away from the face.

questions.q: Why did Winston's fish come out pale and greasy?
o: The oil was so hot that it could not soak into the fish
The fish was coated in far too much flour and egg
The pot was less than half full of oil, so it cooled quickly
Too much cold, wet fish dropped the oil's heat
questions.why: A big load of cold, wet food drops the oil temperature. Food cooks slowly in cool oil and soaks it up instead of crisping. Fry in small batches and let the oil heat again between them.

questions.q: What does the dark, foaming oil tell Winston?
o: It is at the perfect heat for frying fish
It has too little salt in it and needs more
It is breaking down and should be changed
It needs only a splash of fresh oil on top
questions.why: Oil that is dark, foams, smells bad or smokes has broken down. It spoils the taste, burns easily and can be a fire risk, so it is changed rather than topped up.

questions.q: What is wrong with the way the pot of oil is filled?
o: It is too empty to cover the fish properly
It is over half full, so hot oil can bubble over
It has no lid on it, which would keep the heat in
It is too deep for the thermometer to give a reading
questions.why: When wet food goes in, oil bubbles up. A pot more than about half full can overflow onto the flame or the floor, causing a fire or a bad burn.

questions.q: Why is the hot vinegar mixture poured over the fried fish?
o: It finishes cooking the raw middle of the thick fillets
It is the escoveitch pickle, which flavours and keeps the fish
It washes the extra oil off the fish before it is served
It brings the fish back up to 74 °C before it is served
questions.why: Escoveitch fish is fried, then covered with a hot pickle of vinegar, onion, carrot and pepper. The vinegar flavours the fish and helps it keep a little longer, but it does not cook it.

questions.q: What should Marva do when the probe reads 68 °C?
o: Serve them, since the golden skin shows they are done
Cover them and let the heat inside carry on cooking while they are served
Put them back in the oven until the thickest part reaches about 74 °C
Remove the skin and serve the chicken with plenty of sauce
questions.why: Skin colour is not a safe guide. Chicken must reach about 74 °C in the thickest part to kill harmful bacteria, so it goes back until the probe shows this.

questions.q: How should the leg quarters be arranged in the tray for even roasting?
o: In a single layer with gaps, on a rack or trivet
Piled up in the middle to keep the heat in
Packed tightly side by side, to stop them drying
Stacked in two layers, with the larger pieces on top
questions.why: Hot air must reach every piece. Overlapping or stacked pieces cook unevenly and stay pale. A rack also lifts the chicken out of its own fat.

questions.q: The cooked chicken must wait 20 minutes for the guests. What is the safest way to hold it?
o: On the warm stove top, uncovered, where it can be seen
Covered, at 63 °C or above, in a hot cupboard
In the fridge, to be reheated just before it is served
On the bench at room temperature, under a sheet of foil
questions.why: Hot food held for service must stay at 63 °C or above, so bacteria cannot grow. A bench is in the danger zone, and a stove top does not hold a steady, safe temperature.

questions.q: Why does the chef tell Neville to steam the callaloo instead of boiling it?
o: It keeps the colour and flavour, with fewer vitamins lost
It is quicker than boiling and needs no salt at all
Boiling makes the leaves toxic if they cook for too long
Steamed leaves keep their flavour without any seasoning
questions.why: In boiling water, vitamins and colour pass out of the leaves into the water. Steaming for a short time keeps most of them and the flavour, without adding fat.

questions.q: What should Neville do about the coconut milk that is starting to split?
o: Add cold water to calm it down
Lower the heat to a gentle simmer and stir
Turn it up higher to finish the sauce faster
Take the lid off and leave it to boil dry
questions.why: Coconut milk splits when it is boiled hard. A low, steady simmer with occasional stirring keeps it smooth as it reduces to the thick, oily run down sauce.

questions.q: When is run down ready?
o: The coconut milk has boiled for exactly five minutes in the pot
The fish has turned golden brown on both of its sides
The coconut milk is thick and oily, and the fish is tender
All the liquid has gone, and the pot has begun to catch
questions.why: Run down is simmered gently until the coconut milk reduces, thickens and turns oily, and the fish is tender. A dry pot means the dish has burnt.

questions.q: Why is the goat still tough after 40 minutes?
o: It was browned first, and browning hardens the meat
The pieces were cut too small to stew in the pot
The curry powder has toughened the muscle fibres
It needs far longer slow cooking in liquid
questions.why: Goat is a tough cut. Connective tissue turns soft only with long, slow cooking in liquid, often 1 to 2 hours or more. Browning only adds flavour and colour.

questions.q: What should Janelle do instead of turning up the heat?
o: Take off the lid and boil it hard to reduce the sauce
Take the meat out and serve it while it is still hot
Keep it covered at a gentle simmer, and test it
Stir in some cold water to slow the pot down a little
questions.why: A hard boil makes the meat tougher and the sauce can catch and burn. Low, steady heat in a covered pot is how tough meat becomes tender; add hot water only if the liquid runs low.

questions.q: The goat is now tender, but the sauce is thin. What can she do?
o: Simmer it without the lid, or add a little roux
Add a large handful of raw flour straight to the pot
Stir in cold milk and bring it to a hard boil
Pour the thin sauce into a jug and serve it apart
questions.why: Reducing by simmering without the lid concentrates the flavour and thickens the sauce. A little roux also helps. Raw flour added to a stew gives lumps and a floury taste.

questions.q: What is the correct first action by someone near the burning pan?
o: Turn off the gas if safe, then smother it with a blanket
Pour water on it from the tap to cool the oil down
Carry the burning pan across the kitchen to the sink
Fan the flames with a cloth to try to blow them out
questions.why: Cutting off the heat and the air puts the fire out. A fire blanket or lid smothers it. Never carry a burning pan, because it can spill and burn you.

questions.q: Why is water the wrong thing to throw on an oil fire?
o: It makes the oil smoke more but burn less fiercely
It cools the oil so slowly that the flames come back
It puts the flame out but leaves the oil poisonous
It sinks, turns to steam and throws burning oil about
questions.why: Water is heavier than oil and sinks beneath it, then flashes into steam and sprays burning oil across the kitchen. Smother the fire instead.

questions.q: After the flames are out, what should happen to the pan?
o: Lift the blanket at once to see how the oil looks
Move it to a cold bench so that it cools more quickly
Put it back on the heat and finish cooking the food
Leave it covered until it is cold, and report it
questions.why: Lifting the cover lets air back in and the fire can restart. Hot oil can re-ignite until it is fully cool. Report the fire, so the cause can be found and the equipment checked.

questions.q: How can you tell onions have been properly sweated?
o: They are soft and glossy, and have not browned
They are crisp and deep brown around the edges
They are hard in the middle and still white outside
They are dry, with all of the fat gone from the pan
questions.why: Sweating means cooking gently in a little fat, with a lid on, until the vegetable is soft and see-through but has taken no colour. Browning means the heat was too high.
